Ask for three years of tax returns before you look at the seller's spreadsheet. If the two disagree, believe the returns.
Seller's discretionary earnings only matter if you can verify every add-back. Ask for receipts behind each one.
A customer that pays more than 20% of revenue is a risk to price in, not a footnote.
Check the lease before you fall in love. A business with 18 months left on its lease is often worth far less than one with ten.
Lenders look at debt service coverage after a market salary for you. Run the numbers that way before you make an offer.
A seller note does more than fill a funding gap. It keeps the seller invested in a smooth handover.
Ask why the owner is selling, then ask the employees, the landlord and the biggest supplier the same question.
If the owner is the only person who knows how to quote, sell or fix things, budget for a longer transition.
Recurring revenue earns higher multiples. Count only revenue that is contracted or reliably repeats.
Working capital is part of the deal. Agree how much stays in the business at closing before you sign the LOI.
Get bank statements straight from the bank portal during diligence, not as PDFs forwarded by the seller.
A letter of intent is mostly non-binding, but exclusivity and confidentiality clauses usually are. Read them twice.
Visit the business on its busiest day and its slowest day. Both tell you something the financials do not.
Ask for monthly revenue for 36 months. Annual totals hide seasonality and recent declines.
If inventory is included, count it near closing and price it at cost, not retail.
Licences and permits do not always transfer. Confirm each one with the issuing authority early.
Owners: clean books are the cheapest way to raise your multiple. Start a year before you plan to sell.
Owners: document your processes now. Buyers pay more for a business that runs without you.
Owners: keep the sale confidential until you have a signed LOI. Early news can scare staff and customers.
Owners: an unsolicited offer is a starting point. Get a valuation before you answer it.
Franchise resales trade on the remaining term. Check how many years are left and the renewal cost.
Read Item 19 of a franchise disclosure document if it exists. If it does not, ask current franchisees about their numbers.
Online businesses: verify traffic and revenue in the live analytics and payment accounts, not screenshots.
Online businesses: check how much traffic comes from one platform. A single algorithm change can halve it.
Budget closing costs of roughly 2–5% of the price for legal, accounting, lender and escrow fees.
A price is only half the deal. Terms such as seller financing, earn-outs and transition help can be worth more.
Talk to at least two lenders before you sign an LOI. Their questions will expose weak points in the deal.
Non-compete and non-solicit clauses protect what you are buying. Make sure they fit the local law.
Plan your first 100 days before closing: who you will meet, what you will not change and what you will measure.
If a deal feels rushed, slow it down. Good businesses survive a careful buyer; weak ones need a hurried one.
